key_insight: A time-series classification approach can predict individual absenteeism from prior attendance patterns, rather than just re-labeling the current moment, and it performs well despite severe class imbalance.
clinical_relevance: This could help healthcare and other high-demand employers plan staffing proactively by identifying higher absence risk earlier, though it is a workforce analytics tool rather than a clinical decision aid.
method: Separated historical attendance sequences from future absence labels using a time-series classification framework.
Compared Binary Focal Loss and Geometric Mean loss under severe class imbalance.
Evaluated LSTM, CNN, and LSTM-FCN models on simulated longitudinal absenteeism data.
evidence_signal: On held-out test data, the best settings achieved about 0.888 balanced accuracy, with BFL reaching specificity 0.813; performance was strongest with batch sizes ≥64 and 40–80 day windows.
watch_item: Results were based on a simulated dataset calibrated to a UCI source, so external validity on real longitudinal attendance data remains uncertain.
paper_title: A time-series classification framework for individual-level absenteeism prediction under severe class imbalance
